Red tree voles (Arborimus longicaudatus) are small, arboreal rodents endemic to the coastal coniferous forests of the Pacific Northwest, and their life history is characterized by a slow pace of life typical of many arvicolines. This low weight at parturition necessitates a prolonged period of intense maternal investment, as the pups are entirely dependent on the mother for warmth and nutrition. This small aggregate mass is consistent with the species' reliance on secure, predator-free nest sites in the forest canopy, where the energetic demands on the mother are relatively low during the immediate post-partum period.

This reproductive strategy appears to be an adaptation to the unpredictable availability of high-quality forage in the conifer canopy.

The transition to nutritional independence occurs when the offspring reach a wet weight of approximately 21 grams [Wwx = approximately 21 grams] at weaning, a benchmark that corresponds to achieving sufficient size to process solid forage. This weaning event typically occurs around 32 days after birth [tx = around 32 days after birth] at 38.1 °C [T = 38.1 °C], aligning with the 30 to 35 day window reported in related species. At this point, the suckling juvenile makes a complete dietary transition from milk to the needles, cones, and bark that constitute the adult diet, a shift that requires the development of both digestive enzymes and the appropriate gut microflora. The post-weaning juvenile enters a period of rapid somatic growth, during which body mass increases substantially as the individual learns to navigate the complex three-dimensional environment of the forest canopy. Mortality rates during this early juvenile stage are relatively high, primarily due to predation by owls and arboreal snakes.

This degree of sexual size dimorphism is common among voles and is generally thought to reflect selective pressures related to fecundity, as larger females can support larger litters. The ultimate body mass is attained after somatic growth has effectively ceased, marking the transition to the adult stage where the majority of metabolic effort shifts toward reproduction.
